user_turns:
My co-founder wants me to fire our VP of Sales by the end of the month, and I'm furious and honestly scared of what this does to us. Yes, Connor was my college roommate. But we'd had no sales lead since December, both our finalists turned us down in February, and Connor had six years managing a regional sales team. I told Jonas I wanted to skip the loop and get him in fast. He said, "It's your side. Your call." He had coffee with Connor and didn't object.

The targets were set in December, before Connor was even hired, and they assumed multi-location scheduling would ship in June. Jonas's team shipped it September 9, three months late. Nine of our lost deals list it as the reason. The month it shipped, Connor's team closed $150k. Our Q4 pipeline is $1.1 million, more than double last year's.

Now Jonas is threatening me: Connor's out by the end of the month or he takes it to the board. He's making Connor the scapegoat. I think he needs someone to blame besides his own team. Am I wrong to want to give Connor one more quarter?

results.result:
You're not wrong to want it. But I think you're arguing the wrong case, and the way you're framing this is going to lose you the argument with Jonas and possibly the board.

Here's the uncomfortable part first.

**"It's your side. Your call" is not co-ownership of the hire.** It's deference. You told your co-founder you wanted to skip the interview loop to fast-track your college roommate, and he let you. That's a shared failure of process, but it's not the same as Jonas endorsing Connor. From where he sits, the story is: Scott bypassed the hiring process for a friend, the friend missed his numbers, and now Scott is explaining why the numbers don't count. Every fact you listed may be true and that story still reads as plausible to anyone outside your head. You need to know that's what you're up against.

**Lost deals always cite a product gap.** Sales blames product, product blames sales, forever. Nine deals listing multi-location scheduling is real evidence, but the question a board will ask is: what did a VP of Sales *do* for three months while that feature was late? Did he re-segment toward single-location customers? Tighten qualification so his team stopped spending cycles on deals that couldn't close? Build the pipeline that's now paying off? If the answer is yes, that's your case. If the answer is "he waited for the feature," that's Jonas's case.

**Six years running a regional sales team is not the same job as first VP of Sales at a startup.** You know this. It doesn't mean Connor can't do it, but "he was qualified" isn't self-evident, and you shouldn't lean on it.

**You and Jonas are both scapegoating.** You think he needs someone to blame besides his own team. He thinks you're protecting a friend. You're both probably a little right. The December targets died the day the ship date slipped, and the honest version of this conversation is two founders admitting the plan broke and resetting together, not one of you collecting the other's head.

Now the part where you have a real argument, and it's not the one you're making.

**Timing.** Your Q4 pipeline is $1.1M and the person who built it is Connor. Firing the head of sales on October 31 with a new sales lead nowhere in sight, after you already failed to hire one for most of a year, is a decision that costs you Q4 regardless of whether Connor is the long-term answer. That's not a loyalty argument. That's a math argument, and it's the one Jonas and the board have to engage with.

**The $150k and the pipeline are a signal, but only if you define what they need to turn into.** Right now they're anecdotes. Make them a test.

What I'd actually do:

Don't fight the ultimatum. Convert it. Go to Jonas and say: you're right that the December targets are dead and you're right that we can't keep running sales without a clear bar. Here's a proposal. Connor gets Q4. We set the number together, now, in writing, adjusted for the actual ship date and the pipeline he's showing. If he misses it, he's out January 15 and I won't fight you. If he hits it, this conversation is over. And we take *that* to the board together, as a joint recommendation, rather than you taking a grievance and me taking a defense.

Then watch how Jonas reacts. If he takes the deal, you've bought the quarter and defused the founder fight. If he refuses a clear, time-boxed test with a pre-committed outcome, one of two things is true: either he's already decided and no evidence will matter, or he knows something about Connor's performance that you haven't heard, in which case ask him directly what he's seeing. Both are worth finding out.

Two more things. Get someone who isn't you to look at Connor's pipeline and his team, ideally a board member or advisor who's run sales. You cannot evaluate your college roommate cleanly and everyone involved knows it, which is exactly why Jonas is escalating instead of trusting your read. An outside look protects Connor if he's good and protects you if he isn't.

And separate the Connor question from the Jonas question. Even if you win this one, a co-founder issuing month-end ultimatums and threatening to go around you to the board is a relationship problem that will outlast Connor. The fear you mentioned is the right thing to be afraid of. Address it directly with him, not through this fight.

No. You're right about one thing and wrong about the thing you're asking me to confirm.

You're right that firing Connor on October 31 is bad timing and that the December targets are a dishonest yardstick. That's a strong, defensible position, and I think you'd win it.

You're not right that Jonas is simply scapegoating and that Connor is being wronged. You don't actually know that yet. You hired your college roommate without a process, you've been grading him on a curve you built, and you haven't gotten a single independent read on whether he's good at this job. You might be correct about him. But "I'm right" isn't a conclusion you're in a position to reach from where you're standing, and the moment you walk into the room with Jonas believing it, you're going to argue about who's to blame instead of what to do, and that fight ends with the board picking a side.

What I laid out isn't a way to prove you're right. It's a way to find out, with a plan that holds up whichever way it goes. If you want one more quarter for Connor, the price is agreeing in advance to what "he failed" looks like and being willing to act on it. If you're not willing to pay that price, then it isn't really about the evidence, and Jonas will be able to tell.
